sentences.text: After the Kalinga war, Ashoka inscribed messages on rocks and polished pillars to proclaim his dhamma, a set of moral principles meant to hold together a vast empire.
Its content was simple: respect for elders, generosity towards Brahmanas and renouncers, kindness to slaves and servants, and respect for other religions.
Though personally a Buddhist, Ashoka did not impose his faith and made gifts even to non-Buddhist sects.
He promised heaven to those who behaved well but never spoke of nirvana, the Buddhist goal.
To spread the message of dhamma, Ashoka appointed special officers called rajukas.
Most edicts used Prakrit in the Brahmi script, while some in the north-west used Kharosthi, Aramaic or Greek.
Dhamma also served the state, for Ashoka retained Kalinga and warned forest peoples against violating the social order.
These edicts, deciphered by James Prinsep in the late 1830s, remain our main source on his ideas.
Ashoka's blend of ethics and statecraft still inspires India, whose national emblem comes from his lion capital at Sarnath.
